overview: The QMC5883L measures the strength of the magnetic field along three axes, which is what lets it work out a heading relative to magnetic north the same way a physical compass needle does. It became the de facto budget breakout chip after largely replacing the older HMC5883L on cheap modules — the two are pin-compatible and often sold under the same silkscreen label, but they use a different I2C address and register map entirely, so code written for one reads garbage from the other. On its own it only gives a heading when held perfectly level; any tilt introduces error unless the reading is tilt-compensated using a separate accelerometer, which is exactly why most robotics projects pair it with (or upgrade to) a combined IMU instead of using it alone.
simpleSummary: A tiny sensor that senses Earth's magnetic field to work out which way is north, like a digital compass needle.

pinMap.name: SDA
pinMap.gotcha: Boards silkscreened 'HMC5883L' sometimes actually carry a QMC5883L die (or vice versa) as manufacturers swap suppliers — the two use different I2C addresses (0x0D vs 0x1E) and register maps, so a library written for one will read nothing or garbage from the other. Confirm which chip you actually have before debugging your code.

pinMap.name: DRDY
pinMap.function: Data-ready interrupt output — pulses when a new measurement is available, letting you skip polling the status register over I2C.
pinMap.gotcha: Often left unconnected on breakout boards — if it never toggles, that's expected unless you've wired it, not a sign the sensor has failed.

useCases.title: Robot compass heading
useCases.scenario: Fuse magnetometer heading with a gyroscope for a stable compass reading that doesn't drift the way pure gyro integration does.

useCases.title: Metal detector / ferrous object trigger
useCases.scenario: Watch for sudden local field distortions caused by a nearby ferrous object passing close to the sensor.

useCases.title: Drone yaw reference
useCases.scenario: Provide an absolute heading reference to correct for gyroscope yaw drift in a flight controller.

useCases.title: Handheld digital compass
useCases.scenario: Simple standalone gadget that displays heading on a small screen.

useCases.title: Non-contact current sensing
useCases.scenario: Roughly estimate current flow through a nearby wire from the magnetic field it generates (coarse, needs calibration).

commonlyPairedWith: MPU6050 (fusing accel+gyro with this magnetometer to build a custom 9-DOF stack)
oftenConfusedWith: HMC5883L (nearly pin-identical breakout, but a different I2C address and register map — firmware for one won't read the other correctly without changes)
MPU9250/BNO055 (this is a bare magnetometer only; those already include a magnetometer alongside a gyroscope and accelerometer in one package)
oftenUpgradedTo: MPU9250, for a full 9-DOF sensor in one part instead of wiring a separate magnetometer
BNO055, for finished sensor-fusion heading output instead of raw magnetometer readings that need your own tilt-compensation and calibration

beginnerMistakes: Mounting it close to motors, speakers, or a steel chassis, which corrupts every reading with local magnetic distortion.
Skipping hard-iron/soft-iron calibration (the figure-8 waving routine), leaving heading off by tens of degrees.
Assuming it's an HMC5883L (or vice versa) and using the wrong library/address for the chip actually on the board.
Forgetting magnetic north isn't true north — the declination angle varies by location and matters for real navigation.
Reading raw axis values without tilt-compensation, so heading is only correct when the sensor is held perfectly level.
